chapters.1: King Ahaziah of Israel is injured in a fall and sends messengers to a foreign god, Baal-zebub, to ask if he will recover. Elijah intercepts them with God's verdict that Ahaziah will die for ignoring Israel's God, and when the king sends soldiers to arrest Elijah, fire from heaven consumes two companies before a humbler third captain gets through. Ahaziah dies as Elijah said, and his brother Jehoram becomes king.
chapters.2: Elijah's ministry ends as he and Elisha cross the Jordan on dry ground, and Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind with a chariot and horses of fire, and Elisha picks up his fallen mantle and immediately performs his first miracle, dividing the Jordan. He then heals a poisoned spring at Jericho and curses a group of mocking youths at Bethel.
chapters.3: Israel's king Jehoram, Judah's king Jehoshaphat, and Edom's king join forces against rebelling Moab, but their armies nearly die of thirst in the desert. Elisha promises water and victory, and a flash flood fills the valley overnight, leading to a rout of the Moabites. The campaign ends abruptly when the desperate Moabite king sacrifices his own son on the city wall, and the allied kings withdraw.
chapters.4: This chapter gathers several of Elisha's miracles: he multiplies a widow's oil to pay off her debt, and promises a childless Shunammite woman a son, who is later born. When that son dies suddenly, Elisha travels to her and raises him back to life. The chapter closes with two provision miracles, Elisha neutralizing poisonous wild gourds in a pot of stew and feeding a hundred men from just twenty loaves of bread.
chapters.5: Naaman, a powerful Syrian military commander with leprosy, is told by a captive Israelite servant girl to seek out Elisha. After an initial insult at being told to simply wash in the Jordan River seven times, Naaman obeys and is healed, and he pledges loyalty to Israel's God. Elisha refuses payment, but his own servant Gehazi lies to get silver and clothing from Naaman, and Elisha pronounces that Naaman's leprosy will now fall on Gehazi.
chapters.6: Elisha performs a small miracle, making a lost iron axe head float so a worker can recover it, then supernaturally reveals Syrian military plans to protect the king of Israel. When Syria sends an army to capture him, Elisha strikes them with temporary blindness and leads them into Samaria, where the king feeds them and sends them home in peace. The chapter ends darkly as Syria besieges Samaria, causing such severe famine that the king is horrified to learn two desperate mothers resorted to cannibalism.
chapters.7: Elisha predicts that the famine-stricken siege of Samaria will end within a day with abundant, cheap food. Four desperate lepers sneak into the Syrian camp expecting to find enemies, but discover the Syrians have fled in panic after hearing a sound God made them think was an approaching army. The lepers report the news, the city plunders the abandoned camp, and the skeptical royal official who doubted Elisha's prophecy is trampled to death exactly as predicted.
chapters.8: The Shunammite woman whose son Elisha raised returns from a famine-driven exile and, with Elisha's former servant Gehazi vouching for her, gets her land restored by the king. Elisha then tells Hazael, an official of Syria's king, that Hazael himself will become king and will bring great harm to Israel; Hazael later smothers his master to take the throne. The chapter also tracks the troubled, idolatrous reigns of Judah's kings Jehoram and his son Ahaziah, both tied by marriage to Ahab's corrupt dynasty.
chapters.9: Elisha sends a young prophet to secretly anoint Jehu as the new king of Israel and commission him to destroy Ahab's dynasty. Jehu immediately moves on this, killing King Joram of Israel and the visiting King Ahaziah of Judah, fulfilling the prophecy about Naboth's vineyard. He then has the wicked queen mother Jezebel thrown from a window, and she is trampled and eaten by dogs exactly as Elijah had once prophesied.
chapters.10: Jehu consolidates his new throne by having Ahab's seventy sons executed and killing off the rest of Ahab's family, officials, and priests, fulfilling God's judgment on that dynasty. He then tricks all the worshippers of Baal into assembling in Baal's temple and has them slaughtered, destroying Baal worship in Israel. However, Jehu never abandons the golden calf idols set up by Jeroboam, so even though God rewards his zeal with a lasting dynasty, Israel's territory begins shrinking under foreign pressure during his reign.
chapters.11: After her son Ahaziah's death, the wicked queen Athaliah seizes the throne of Judah and kills off the royal family, but the infant prince Joash is secretly rescued and hidden in the temple for six years. The priest Jehoiada then organizes a coup, crowning the boy-king Joash and having Athaliah put to death. The people tear down the temple of Baal, and Judah's throne is restored to David's line.
chapters.12: The boy-king Joash reigns well under the priest Jehoiada's early guidance and organizes the repair of the Jerusalem temple, which had fallen into disrepair, using donations collected in a chest by the door. When the Syrian king Hazael threatens Jerusalem, Joash pays him off with treasures from the temple and palace rather than fight. Despite his earlier faithfulness, Joash is eventually assassinated by his own servants.
chapters.13: In Israel, kings Jehoahaz and Jehoash both continue in Jeroboam's idolatry while Syria oppresses the nation, though Jehoahaz's prayer brings some relief. The chapter records the death of Elisha, whose dying act is a symbolic prophecy of victory over Syria using a bow and arrows, and even his bones later revive a dead man. The chapter closes noting that God's enduring covenant kept Israel from total destruction despite the nation's unfaithfulness.
chapters.14: Judah's king Amaziah defeats Edom but then foolishly provokes Israel's king Jehoash into a war that ends in Judah's humiliating defeat and the plundering of Jerusalem; Amaziah is later assassinated. His son Azariah (Uzziah) becomes king of Judah, while in Israel, Jeroboam II reigns for over forty years and restores Israel's borders, even though the text says he continued in sin, because God still had compassion on suffering Israel.
chapters.15: This chapter rapidly tracks a chaotic period in Israel's history, where king after king is assassinated in quick succession (Zachariah, Shallum, Pekahiah) by Menahem, Pekah, and others, mostly as Assyria's power begins pressing on the region. Meanwhile in Judah, Azariah (Uzziah) reigns long but is struck with leprosy, and his son Jotham later reigns well but still tolerates pagan worship sites.
chapters.16: Ahaz becomes king of Judah and leads the nation into deep idolatry, even sacrificing his own son and setting up a pagan-style altar copied from Damascus in place of temple worship patterns. Under pressure from Syria and Israel, he appeals to Assyria for help, paying tribute with temple treasures and effectively becoming Assyria's vassal. This submission draws Judah more tightly into Assyria's political and religious orbit.
chapters.17: The northern kingdom of Israel falls as Assyria conquers Samaria and deports the Israelite population, ending the ten-tribe kingdom for good. The chapter explains this collapse theologically: it happened because Israel persistently worshipped idols and ignored the prophets despite repeated warnings. Assyria resettles the land with foreign peoples who adopt a mixed religion, worshipping the Lord alongside their own gods, becoming the ancestors of the later Samaritans.
chapters.18: Hezekiah becomes king of Judah and leads major religious reforms, removing idols and trusting God rather than foreign alliances. Assyria's king Sennacherib invades Judah, and his field commander Rabshakeh stands outside Jerusalem's walls mocking Hezekiah's faith and urging the people to surrender, claiming no god can save them from Assyria.
chapters.19: Hezekiah responds to Assyria's threats by seeking the prophet Isaiah and praying earnestly in the temple for deliverance. Isaiah delivers God's assurance that Sennacherib will fail and return home. That night the angel of the Lord strikes down the Assyrian army, and Sennacherib retreats to Nineveh, where he is later assassinated by his own sons.
chapters.20: Hezekiah becomes terminally ill, but after he weeps and prays, God grants him fifteen more years of life, confirmed by a miraculous sign of the sun's shadow moving backward. Later, Hezekiah proudly shows off his treasures to visiting Babylonian envoys, and Isaiah warns him that Babylon will one day carry off those very treasures and his descendants into exile.
chapters.21: Hezekiah's son Manasseh becomes one of Judah's worst kings, reversing his father's reforms, filling Jerusalem with idolatry and even child sacrifice, and shedding much innocent blood. God announces through the prophets that Judah will face the same judgment as Israel because of this. Manasseh's son Amon continues this idolatry briefly before being assassinated, and the boy Josiah succeeds him.
chapters.22: The young king Josiah orders repairs to the Jerusalem temple, during which the high priest Hilkiah discovers a long-lost scroll of the Law. When it is read to Josiah, he is deeply shaken by how far the nation has strayed and sends to the prophetess Huldah, who confirms that judgment is coming but that Josiah himself, because of his humble response, will not live to see the worst of it.
chapters.23: Josiah gathers the nation to publicly renew their covenant with God, then leads a sweeping reform, destroying idols, pagan altars, and corrupt priesthoods throughout Judah and even in parts of the former northern kingdom. He also restores the Passover celebration on a grand scale. Despite being called the most devoted king since David, Josiah is later killed in battle against Egypt, and his sons Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim briefly and unfaithfully succeed him under foreign domination.
chapters.24: Babylon's power rises under Nebuchadnezzar, who makes Judah's king Jehoiakim a vassal and later besieges Jerusalem again under Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin, deporting him and much of the population and treasury to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar installs Zedekiah as a puppet king, but Zedekiah eventually rebels against Babylon, setting up the kingdom's final collapse.
chapters.25: Babylon besieges and finally destroys Jerusalem, burning the temple and palace, tearing down the city walls, and carrying most of the remaining population into exile, ending the kingdom of Judah. A Babylonian-appointed governor, Gedaliah, is soon assassinated, and many survivors flee to Egypt in fear. The book ends on a small note of hope as the exiled former king Jehoiachin is later shown kindness and given a regular place at the Babylonian king's table.
